Silicon Carbide (SiC) Heating Element Guide

A practical, engineering-first guide to silicon carbide heating elements — what they are, how they work, and how to specify them.

On this page

  • What they are
  • How they work
  • Configurations
  • Temperature range
  • Ageing
  • Selecting
  • Replacing

What is a silicon carbide heating element?

A silicon carbide (SiC) heating element is an electrical resistance heater made from silicon carbide. When current passes through it, its resistance converts electrical energy into heat, which radiates into the furnace. SiC elements are widely used for high-temperature electric furnaces operating in air.

They are made with a resistive hot zone in the middle and low-resistance cold ends that pass through the furnace wall to the electrical terminals. Common forms include straight rods, U-type, W-type, spiral and dumbbell shapes — see the full range of SiC heating elements.

How does a SiC heating element work?

Heat generation follows Ohm's law: for a given supply voltage V and element resistance R, the power dissipated is P = V²/R. The cold ends are made with a much lower resistance than the hot zone (through larger cross-section or a lower-resistivity end), so almost all the heat is produced in the hot zone while the ends and furnace wall stay cooler.

SiC resistance is not constant with temperature. It falls from room temperature to a minimum in the mid-temperature range, then rises again at high temperature. This is why the cold resistance of an element differs from its operating resistance.

Configurations

The hot-zone shape is chosen for the furnace layout and electrical requirement:

  • Straight — single hot zone, the most common form.
  • U-type / W-type — both terminals on one side; W extends the hot zone.
  • Spiral — machined hot zone for higher resistance / higher voltage.
  • Dumbbell — thick cold ends, thinner hot zone, heat focused in the centre.
  • Alpha SiC — dense recrystallised grade, often for higher temperatures.

Temperature range

SiC elements are used across a broad high-temperature range in air. The usable maximum depends on the element grade, the surface loading (watts per unit area) and the furnace design, so it should be confirmed per application rather than assumed. As a rule of thumb, higher operating temperatures call for higher-grade material and more conservative loading.

We don't publish a single guaranteed maximum — tell us your furnace temperature and we confirm a suitable specification. Try the element calculator for indicative figures.

Ageing — why resistance increases

SiC elements age in service: their resistance gradually increases over time, mainly due to slow oxidation of the silicon carbide. As resistance rises, the same voltage delivers less power, so the furnace can struggle to reach temperature. Systems with tap-changing transformers or variable output let you raise the voltage to compensate as elements age.

Selecting an element

Selection balances geometry (diameter, hot-zone and overall length), the electrical supply (voltage), and the required power and temperature. See how to select a SiC heating element for a step-by-step approach.

Replacing an element

When replacing, elements of similar resistance are usually grouped so the bank heats evenly. If you don't have the original part number, dimensions or a photograph are enough to identify a match — see SiC heater replacement.

FAQs

Frequently asked questions

How long do SiC heating elements last?

Life depends on operating temperature, surface loading, atmosphere, cycling and how the furnace is controlled. Because resistance rises with age, elements are usually replaced when the control system can no longer maintain temperature. We can advise on extending life through loading and control.

Can SiC elements run in any atmosphere?

SiC elements are most commonly used in air. Other atmospheres can affect life and usable temperature — tell us your atmosphere and we'll advise.
